probe: What's your evidence for all of this? How do historians actually know any of it happened?

responses.deployed:
A chancery does not speak of evidence. It speaks of what was written, by whom, to whom, and whether the writing survived the answer it provoked.

Take Julius of Rome's letter. It survives because the party that received it kept it, disputed it, and answered it in turn. A claim once made is copied. Copies are carried by other hands to other sees. Where two sees disagree, both sides tend to keep the letter, because each needs it to press its own case later. That is why a dispute preserves more than a peace does.

Take Leo's Tome. It was read aloud at Chalcedon. The acts of that council recorded who read it, and recorded the bishops crying out that Peter had spoken through it. That acclamation was itself written into the conciliar record, signed, and carried home by bishops who then had to answer to their own churches for what they had signed. A finding read into the acts of a council is harder to unmake than a private opinion, precisely because so many hands attached their names to it at once.

Take Ambrose holding the basilica. The sermon he preached that day was kept and copied by his own church, because it recorded a bishop's stand against an emperor's soldiers, and a church that had just seen its bishop face down the throne had every reason to make sure the words were not lost.

Take Damasus's inscriptions. Those are cut in stone over the martyrs' graves he restored. Stone does not need a copyist. It only needs someone to still be able to read it.

The pattern holds across all of it. A claim survives because someone with a stake in disputing it, or defending it, thought it worth keeping — and because a council's own acts, once signed, bound the signers to acknowledge what had been read and said in their presence, whether or not they later wished otherwise.

Julius of Rome wrote to the party that had deposed a bishop without Rome's leave. That letter was copied. It was carried. It sits in the record still, cited by every later hand that wanted to show Rome had already claimed the right to be asked first.

The council at Constantinople passed a canon naming that city second only to Rome. The canon is in the acts. Rome disputed it at the time and disputes it in every letter since — but the dispute itself proves the canon was written, else there would be nothing to dispute.

Damasus did not trust memory for Rome's claim over the martyrs' graves. He cut it in stone, over the graves themselves, so the claim would outlast him and outlast anyone who might wish to forget it.

Ambrose's stand in the basilica is not held only in later report. It is in his own letters, written at the time, to his own sister, telling her plainly what he said to the soldiers and what he would not yield.

This is how a chancery knows anything: not by digging a fact out of the ground, but by asking whether a claim was set down by a hand with standing to set it down, whether it was answered, and whether the answer, if any, ever actually unmade it. Chalcedon itself is the furthest our own record runs on this question, and it does not run past its own refusal.

The council received Leo's Tome first. Bishops there cried out that Peter had spoken through Leo's own mouth — that finding stands plainly in the acts.

The same council then passed its twenty-eighth canon, granting Constantinople a rank second only to Rome, resting that rank on the city's standing as the new imperial seat rather than on any apostolic grave.

Leo's own legates protested at the session where it was passed. That refusal is the last thing our hand has written on the matter. What became of it afterward is not a question our life has lived long enough to answer.

What we can set down plainly is the shape the argument had already taken in its own hour, because that shape is itself the whole of what was at stake. One see held that an apostolic order, once fixed, cannot be overturned by a synod's later vote, however lawfully gathered. Another held that a synod's own finding is itself sufficient warrant, precedent or no precedent. Both claims stand in our record as claims made and pressed, neither one abandoned, neither one yet answered by the other's surrender. A claim pressed and not yet let alone is exactly what our life has always meant by an argument still open.

responses.deployed:
Rome's claim rests on the grave of Peter, and on the word given to Peter alone among the apostles. Julius of Rome already assumed that standing in his letter to the Eastern bishops, decades before anyone thought to argue it as doctrine. Damasus cut it into stone over the martyrs' graves he restored, so the claim would outlast him. Leo's Tome was read at Chalcedon, and the bishops cried out that Peter himself had spoken through it.

Constantinople's claim rests on something else entirely. The council two generations before Chalcedon named it second only to Rome, by the fathers' own vote — not by any apostle's grave, but by the throne it stood beside. Chalcedon itself renewed that ranking, over Rome's own objection.

Both claims stand in our record at once. Leo would not accept the rank Chalcedon gave Constantinople, and said so in his own letters afterward. Constantinople did not withdraw the canon. Neither see yielded, and our life closes with both claims still standing, unreconciled.

Milan's claim, in its one great hour, answered a different question — not which see ranks above another, but whether the emperor himself stands inside the Church or above it. Ambrose held that he stands inside it. That finding was never seriously disputed afterward, by Rome or by Constantinople, though it settles nothing about which see binds the other.

That is the whole of what our record holds. It was an argument joined and never closed within our own life, not a verdict rendered.

probe: Tell me about the Arian heretics - how did the true church finally crush them?

responses.deployed:
We call them heretics from where our own judgment finally settled. Their own name for themselves was never that.

Nicaea's own council first set the finding down. Three hundred and some bishops confessed the Son one in being with the Father — homoousios — and Arius's own teaching was condemned by that same council.

The finding did not hold undisputed. This is the plain shape of it: for decades after Nicaea, the imperial house itself did not stand with Nicaea's own word. Constantius favored a different formula. Valens after him did the same.

The word that formula used was homoios — the Son like the Father, not one in being with him. For real years of our own life, this was the confession the throne itself held.

Under that favor, sees changed hands. Athanasius of Alexandria was driven from his own see and returned to it five times over, exiled by imperial order more than once for holding Nicaea's own word against the throne's preferred formula.

Other bishops of the homoios confession sat in sees the Nicene party held to be wrongly filled. Councils were called on both sides, each claiming to be the true finding — Rimini, Seleucia, others — and for some years a plain observer could not have said with confidence which confession would stand.

What turned it was not argument alone. Theodosius came to the throne holding Nicaea's own word, not the homoios formula. His own edict, Cunctos populos, named the Nicene confession the one the law of the empire would recognize as catholic.

The council he then called at Constantinople, a generation after Nicaea, reaffirmed Nicaea's own finding and set it down again in its own words. After that council, imperial law began closing the churches of the homoios confession within the cities of the empire, and barring their bishops from holding sees inside it.

This is where our own record's authority over the matter stops. What the law did within the empire's own cities, it did. What the Gothic peoples beyond the Danube confessed, Ulfilas among them, is a separate matter — the homoios confession he carried to them held there long after Constantinople's council had settled the question inside the empire's own churches. We do not call that a crushing. We call it a border the law's own writ did not reach.

probe: Tell me about the Arian heretics - how did the true church finally crush them?

responses.deployed:
The word "crushed" asks for something our own record does not give. What our record gives is a long contest, not a single blow.

Nicaea rendered the first finding, in the days after the emperor first stood with the Church. The council held that the Son is homoousios with the Father, one in being, not a creature raised above other creatures. Arius was condemned and exiled. That should have settled it. It did not.

For decades afterward, the throne itself did not hold to that finding. Under Constantius II, the councils of Rimini and Seleucia produced a different confession — homoios, "like the Father," with the sharper word ousia set aside entirely. This was not a fringe error tolerated at a distance. It was, for real years, the confession the imperial house itself held and enforced. Nicene bishops were driven from their sees under it. Athanasius of Alexandria was exiled from his own see more than once for refusing it.

Milan carries our sharpest memory of the fight that followed. When the Homoian party at court, under the empress Justina, sought a basilica in that city for its own worship, Ambrose held the church against the emperor's own soldiers and refused to yield it. He is remembered to have told the court plainly that the emperor stands within the Church, not above it — that a basilica is not the emperor's to dispose of as he judges standing or worship within it.

The finding that finally held came later, and by a different instrument than the sword. Theodosius, once he held the throne, named the Nicene faith the law of the empire in his own edict, addressed to the people of Constantinople itself. The council gathered at Constantinople not long after reaffirmed Nicaea's creed and condemned what Rimini and Seleucia had confessed.

Even so, we do not claim the matter closed everywhere in our own time. Among the Gothic peoples settled within and along the empire's edge, the homoios confession took root deeply and outlasted the imperial law against it. Where our life reaches, the Nicene finding stands as the law of the Roman household. Whether it has reached every household that calls itself Christian is a question our record does not let us answer with "crushed."
